conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here.  
To get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us. My only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported.

When you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt a bit flat or forced?

Hi, Maya. Um… I guess some things still feel nice—like when the baby grips my finger or when my husband brings me coffee—but it’s not the same warm rush I used to get. It’s more… flat, like you said. I’ll smile, but then the feeling kind of fades quickly and I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I mean, I can still laugh sometimes—like yesterday when my sister sent a goofy meme—but it feels kind of forced, like I’m reminding myself “oh, this is funny, I should laugh.” It doesn’t bubble up the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I’ll tell myself, “It’ll be nice to get out for a walk tomorrow,” but when the time comes it feels like one more chore. I still go, and parts are okay, yet the excited flutter I used to have—like before my favorite café or a visit with friends—just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking, “Maybe I didn’t burp him right,” or “My milk might not be good enough.” Deep down I know it’s probably not my fault, but those thoughts still pop up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be sitting on the couch, everything’s quiet, and suddenly my chest feels tight—like I’m waiting for something bad to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. I’ll check the baby three times in ten minutes just to be sure he’s breathing. The worry drifts away pretty quickly, but it keeps coming back out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice this week, yeah. Like yesterday morning—I was changing her diaper, everything routine—and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt shaky, like I might drop her. I had to put her in the crib and sit down until it passed. It lasted maybe a minute, but it left me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I keep things under control, but by late afternoon it can feel like the dishes, laundry, and baby’s next feed are all piling up at once. I’ll think, “I can’t do one more thing,” yet I still manage. It just feels heavier than it used to—like I’m carrying a backpack full of bricks while everyone else is strolling along.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I get pretty tired, so once I finally lie down I’m out pretty quick. Sometimes it takes me a bit to fall asleep because my mind keeps running through the next day, but I wouldn’t say it’s because I’m really unhappy—more just wound-up.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel kind of sad some days. Nothing huge—just this low, heavy feeling that tags along while I’m folding laundry or feeding her. It isn’t constant, but it’s there enough that I notice I’m not my usual self.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve teared up a couple of times this week—like two nights ago when the baby wouldn’t settle and my husband was still at work. I put her down in the crib, went to the bathroom, and just cried for maybe a minute. It wasn’t sobbing or anything, just quiet tears because everything felt a bit much right then.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed or low, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel like “me” again and be okay for my baby.

You've shared that the past two weeks have felt heavy: the things that used to bring easy joy now feel flat or forced, and even planning a simple walk can feel like one more chore. You're coping and completing tasks, yet you describe a constant low mood, sudden waves of worry or panic, and frequent self-blame when the baby is fussy. You've had brief tearful moments, but you've also stayed connected to your little one and your support system, and you clearly state you have no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient reports laughter feels forced and diminished compared to before, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient still participates but reports the anticipatory joy is "just isn't there," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame 'some of the time' with specific examples, matching 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Response describes recurring, unprovoked anxiety episodes occurring "sometimes" with physical symptoms and compulsive checking, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes sudden, unexpected panic symptoms (racing heart, shaking) occurring once or twice this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent daily overwhelm that feels heavier than before, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you above the standard cutoff indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse key symptoms such as <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>episodic panic</sym>, and <sym>diurnal mood variation</sym>, present most days for two weeks, consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and, if needed, medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a short re-screen in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
4. Share results with your partner or trusted support person so they can help with practical tasks and emotional encouragement
5. Practice brief self-care routines-five-minute breathing breaks, outdoor daylight, hydration-to reduce <sym>anxiety spikes</sym>
6. Maintain regular pediatric check-ups; bring a list of questions if worries about the baby resurface
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Patient-reported symptoms (2 wks post-delivery):
- Persistent low mood, heaviness, intermittent tearfulness  
- Marked reduction in capacity for pleasure/anticipation; laughter feels “forced”  
- Daily self-blame/guilt re infant care (“milk not good enough”)  
- Recurrent unprovoked anxiety (tight chest, “waiting for something bad”) with compulsive checking of infant breathing  
- Two sudden panic-like episodes (racing heart, trembling) while caring for infant; resolved <1 min, no safety compromise  
- End-of-day sense of being overwhelmed, “carrying bricks,” though tasks completed  
- No current sleep-onset problems; occasional racing thoughts at bedtime  
- Denies any thoughts of self-harm

Screening significance:
Pattern consistent with sub-threshold to mild depressive symptoms plus prominent anxiety features. No safety concerns voiced. Consider further evaluation with EPDS and clinical interview to clarify diagnostic picture and determine support/intervention needs.
